entry: Application of one's own [[Culture|culture]] as the standard for judging other cultures, practices, beliefs and peoples, usually negatively. The term was first applied in the [[Social science|social sciences]] by American sociologist William G. Sumner, who in his 1906 book *Folkways* called it "the technical name for the view of things in which one's own group is the center of everything, and all others are scaled and rated with reference to it." Some people use the term for the belief that one's culture is superior to all others, especially in language, behavior, customs and religion. It is sometimes related to [[Racism|racism]], stereotyping, [[Discrimination|discrimination]] or xenophobia, though it does not necessarily involve a negative view of others' race. Its opposite is cultural relativism, which holds that a culture is best understood from its own perspective. In *The Authoritarian Personality*, [[Theodor W. Adorno]] and colleagues of the Frankfurt School defined it as combining a positive attitude toward one's in-group with a negative attitude toward the out-group.

Branch of [[Anthropology|anthropology]] devoted to the systematic study of individual cultures from the viewpoint of their members. Ethnographers rely heavily on participant observation, in which the researcher takes part in a setting, often in a marginal role, to document patterns of social interaction and participants' perspectives. Ethnographers mainly use qualitative methods, though they may include quantitative data, and a typical study is holistic, including a brief history and an analysis of the terrain, climate and habitat. The method originated in social and cultural anthropology in the early 20th century and spread notably to [[Sociology|sociology]]. Studied groups include traditional communities, youth gangs, religious cults and organizations. Some studies rely on interviews or documents, as in research on the [[NASA]] Challenger disaster, and online "virtual" settings are studied through netnography. *Histories* by [[Herodotus]] is the usual starting point for ancient ethnographic writing.

Academic discipline that compares and analyzes the characteristics of different peoples and the relationships between them. Unlike [[Ethnography|ethnography]], which studies single groups through direct contact with their culture, ethnology compares and contrasts the research ethnographers have compiled. The term was used and defined by Adam Franz Kollár in a work published in Vienna in 1783. It has been considered an academic field since the late 18th century. Among its goals have been reconstructing human history, identifying cultural invariants such as the incest taboo, and formulating generalizations about [[Human nature|human nature]], a concept criticized since the 19th century. Cultural anthropology became dominant in the United States and [[Social anthropology|social anthropology]] in Great Britain, and the distinction between the three terms is increasingly blurred. The progress of the field, for example through [[Claude Lévi-Strauss]]'s structural anthropology, led to criticism of linear progress models.

Branch of [[Zoology|zoology]] that studies the behavior of non-human animals. Its roots lie in the work of [[Charles Darwin]] and of American and German ornithologists of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The modern discipline is generally considered to have begun in the 1930s with Dutch biologist Nikolaas Tinbergen and Austrian biologists [[Konrad Lorenz]] and Karl von Frisch, who shared the 1973 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physiology or Medicine. Ethology combines laboratory and field science and has strong ties to neuroanatomy, [[Ecology|ecology]] and [[Evolution|evolutionary biology]]. Tinbergen argued that any behavior requires four kinds of explanation: causation, development, evolutionary history and function (adaptive value). E. O. Wilson's *Sociobiology: The New Synthesis* (1975) shifted the field toward social aspects of behavior.

Flammable, colorless [[Organic compound|organic compound]] (CH₃CO₂CH₂CH₃), the [[Ester|ester]] of [[Ethanol|ethanol]] and [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]]. It has a sweet smell similar to pear drops and is used mainly as a low-cost, low-toxicity solvent, including in glues, nail polish removers and the decaffeination of [[Tea|tea]] and [[Coffee|coffee]]. An estimated 1.3 million tonnes were produced worldwide in 2004, mainly by Fischer esterification of ethanol and acetic acid. It is the most common ester in [[Wine|wine]], formed during fermentation.

Colorless, flammable gas (C₂H₄), the simplest [[Alkene|alkene]] and a [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbon]]. Its worldwide production, over 225 million tonnes in 2022, exceeds that of any other [[Organic compound|organic compound]]. Much of it is made into [[Polyethylene|polyethylene]], a widely used plastic. Ethylene is also an important natural [[Plant hormone|plant hormone]] and is used in agriculture to induce ripening of [[Fruit|fruit]]. Industrially it is produced mainly by steam cracking of hydrocarbons heated to 750–950 °C; when [[Ethane|ethane]] is the feedstock, ethylene is the product. Its carbon–carbon double bond is a region of high electron density, making it susceptible to attack by electrophiles, and many of its reactions are catalyzed by transition metals. The hydrate of ethylene is [[Ethanol|ethanol]].

Odorless, colorless, viscous [[Organic compound|organic compound]], the simplest vicinal diol (ethane-1,2-diol). It is mainly used as a raw material for [[Polyester|polyester]] fibers and as antifreeze. It is produced from [[Ethylene|ethylene]] through ethylene oxide, which reacts with water, with yields of 90% achievable. World production was about 20 million tonnes in 2010. It has a sweet taste but is [[Toxicity|toxic]] in high concentrations.

White, slightly water-soluble aminopolycarboxylic acid (EDTA). It binds [[Iron|iron]] and [[Calcium|calcium]] ions, forming water-soluble complexes even at neutral pH, and is used to sequester metal ions in industry, including in [[Textile|textile]] dyeing and pulp and paper bleaching. It softens water in laundry, dissolves scale in boilers, and is often found in cleaning solutions. An iron complex removes [[Hydrogen sulfide|hydrogen sulfide]] from gas streams, and EDTA helps supply iron in agriculture, including hydroponics.

Customary code of polite behavior within a [[Society|society]], [[Social class|social class]] or social group. The French word *étiquette*, meaning label or ticket, dates in English from 1750. In the third millennium BC, Egyptian vizier Ptahhotep's *The Maxims of Ptahhotep* (2375–2350 BC) advised civil virtues such as truthfulness, self-control and kindness. The works of [[Confucius]] emphasized personal and governmental [[Morality|morality]] and the correctness of social relationships. Baldassare Castiglione's *The Book of the Courtier* (1528) addressed courtly etiquette and morality in the Italian Renaissance. [[Louis XIV]] used codified etiquette to tame the French nobility and impress foreign dignitaries at the [[Palace of Versailles]]. As a youth, [[George Washington]] copied out 110 maxims titled *Rules of Civility & Decent Behaviour in Company and Conversation*, which shaped his public persona.

English fee-charging boarding school for boys aged 13–18, in Eton, Berkshire, adjacent to [[Windsor Castle]]. Founded in 1440 by Henry VI, it was originally a charity feeder school for King's College, Cambridge. It is the largest boarding school in England and one of three public schools, with Harrow and Radley, to retain a boys-only, boarding-only tradition. Its alumni include twenty British prime ministers, from Robert Walpole to [[Boris Johnson]]. Pupils wear tailcoats as a daily uniform, and fagging was abolished in 1980.

Pre-Roman civilization of Etruria in ancient [[Italy]], a federation of [[City-state|city-states]] with a common language and culture. Scholars consider the Etruscans an indigenous population, and the earliest identifiably Etruscan culture dates from about 900 BC, in the [[Iron Age]] Villanovan culture. At its greatest extent, its territory covered roughly what is now [[Tuscany]], western Umbria, northern [[Lazio]], the Po Valley and parts of Lombardy and Veneto. Its territory peaked around 500 BC. From the late 4th century BC it succumbed to expanding [[Rome]] in the Roman–Etruscan Wars; Etruscans were granted Roman citizenship in 90 BC, and by 27 BC the whole territory had been incorporated into the [[Roman Empire]]. Elite families grew rich through trade with the [[Celts]] and Greeks, filling their tombs with imported luxuries. Their writing derived from the Euboean alphabet, and the language remains only partly understood.

Study of the origin and evolution of words, including their units of sound and meaning. A subfield of [[Linguistics|linguistics]] closely tied to [[Historical linguistics|historical linguistics]], philology and [[Semiotics|semiotics]], etymology uses texts about languages with long written histories. Etymologists apply the [[Comparative linguistics|comparative method]] to reconstruct forms too old to be documented, tracing many European word roots to Indo-European. The word derives from Greek *étymon*, meaning "true sense," and *-logia*, "study of." An etymon is the source of a later word, and a reflex is its descendant in a daughter language. Cognates are words inherited in direct descent from a common parent language; doublets are cognates within one language that entered by different routes.

Genus of more than 700 species of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family [[Myrtaceae]]. Most species are trees, often mallees, and a few are shrubs. Together with related genera such as *Corymbia* and *Angophora*, they are commonly called eucalypts or "gum trees." The name, from Greek *eû* ("well") and *kaluptós* ("covered"), refers to the sepals and petals fused into a cap over the stamens. Most species are native to [[Australia]], and every state and territory has representative species. Many have been planted worldwide for fast growth, valuable timber, pulpwood, [[Honey|honey]] production and essential oils, but in some countries they have been removed because their high flammability makes forest fires dangerous. Eucalypts provide habitat and food for wildlife, including the [[Koala]]. *Eucalyptus regnans* is the tallest known flowering plant on Earth.

[[Christianity|Christian]] rite, considered a sacrament in most churches, also called Holy Communion, the Blessed Sacrament or the Lord's Supper. Christians believe that [[Jesus]] instituted the rite at the Last Supper, giving his disciples bread and wine and commanding them to "do this in memory of me." According to the synoptic Gospels, it took place at a [[Passover]] meal. Consecrated bread and wine, or grape juice among some denominations, are consumed on an [[Altar|altar]] or communion table. The [[Catholic Church]] teaches that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ while their appearance is unchanged (transubstantiation), and Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches also affirm an objective change. Lutherans hold that Christ is present "in, with, and under" the forms, while Reformed Christians believe in a real spiritual presence. Plymouth Brethren view the Lord's Supper as a memorial. The term Eucharist is used by Eastern Orthodox, Catholics, Anglicans, Presbyterians and Lutherans, while Latter-day Saints call it the Sacrament.

Mathematical treatise by [[Euclid]] (c. 300 BC). The oldest extant large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics, *Elements* is a collection in 13 books of definitions, postulates, constructions and theorems with proofs. It covers plane and solid [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean geometry]], elementary number theory and incommensurability, including the [[Pythagorean theorem|Pythagorean theorem]], the [[Euclidean algorithm|Euclidean algorithm]] and the proof that infinitely many primes exist, [[Euclid's theorem]]. Drawing on earlier mathematicians such as Hippocrates of Chios, Eudoxus of Cnidus and Theaetetus, it was long used as an introductory geometry textbook and is often called the most successful textbook ever written. Translated into [[Arabic]] and Latin in the medieval period, it strongly influenced mathematics in the medieval Islamic world and Western Europe, and its logical rigor was not surpassed until the 19th century. First printed in 1482, it has had more than 2,000 editions and translations.

Fundamental result of [[Number theory|number theory]] that there are infinitely many [[Prime number|prime numbers]]. First proven by [[Euclid]] in *Elements* (Book IX, Proposition 20), it has at least 200 proofs. Euclid's argument shows that the product of any finite list of primes plus one has a prime factor not on the list. Though often described as a proof by contradiction, it is a direct proof by cases. [[Leonhard Euler]]'s proof uses the [[Fundamental theorem of arithmetic|fundamental theorem of arithmetic]] and expands a product over primes as a [[Geometric series|geometric series]], which shows that there are more primes than squares.

Efficient [[Algorithm|algorithm]] for computing the greatest common divisor of two [[Integer|integers]]. Named after the ancient Greek mathematician [[Euclid]], who described it in his *Elements* (c. 300 BC), it is one of the oldest algorithms in common use. It rests on the principle that the greatest common divisor does not change if the larger number is replaced by its remainder when divided by the smaller. Repeating this produces smaller pairs until the remainder is zero. The number of steps never exceeds five times the number of base-10 digits of the smaller integer, a result proven by Gabriel Lamé in 1844 that marks the beginning of [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity theory]]. The algorithm reduces fractions, performs division in [[Modular arithmetic|modular arithmetic]], helps solve [[Diophantine equation|Diophantine equations]] and forms part of the cryptographic protocols that secure the [[Internet]].

Mathematical system attributed to [[Euclid]], deriving theorems from a small set of axioms. Set out in Euclid's *Elements*, it begins with plane geometry, still taught in secondary school as the first axiomatic system, and goes on to solid geometry of three dimensions. Euclid's five postulates, including the parallel postulate, seemed so intuitively obvious that their theorems were considered absolutely true for more than two thousand years. Two self-consistent [[Non-Euclidean geometry|non-Euclidean geometries]], hyperbolic and elliptic, are now known. An implication of [[Albert Einstein]]'s general relativity is that physical space itself is not Euclidean, although Euclidean space approximates it over short distances and weak gravity. Euclidean geometry is synthetic, proceeding logically from axioms, in contrast to [[Analytic geometry|analytic geometry]], introduced almost 2,000 years later by [[René Descartes]], which uses coordinates.

Two-dimensional [[Euclidean space|Euclidean space]], with positions given by two real numbers. It is an affine space in which parallel lines exist, with metrical properties such as distance, circles and angle measurement. A Euclidean plane with a chosen [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinate system]] is called a Cartesian plane. The real coordinate plane ℝ², with the dot product, is often called the standard Euclidean plane, since every Euclidean plane is isomorphic to it. Books I through IV and VI of Euclid's *Elements* dealt with two-dimensional geometry, including the [[Pythagorean theorem|Pythagorean theorem]]. René Descartes and [[Pierre de Fermat|Pierre de Fermat]] developed coordinates in 1637, but the pair of fixed axes was introduced after Descartes's *La Géométrie* was translated into Latin in 1649. Later the plane was regarded as a field, known as the complex plane and sometimes called the Argand plane after Jean-Robert Argand.

Fundamental space of [[Geometry|geometry]], intended to represent physical space. Originally the three-dimensional space of [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean geometry]], it is defined in modern mathematics for any positive integer dimension n, denoted Eⁿ. Euclidean spaces of a given dimension are all isomorphic, so each can be represented by real n-space ℝⁿ with the standard dot product. Mathematicians did not apply Euclidean geometry to spaces of more than three dimensions until the 19th century.

Geometric object with magnitude (length) and direction, depicted as an arrow between two points. Euclidean vectors can be added and scaled to form a [[Vector space|vector space]], obeying the familiar laws of commutativity, associativity and distributivity. The term was introduced by [[William Rowan Hamilton]] as part of the [[Quaternion|quaternion]], a sum of a real number and a three-dimensional vector. Vectors are essential in [[Physics|physics]]: the velocity and acceleration of a moving object and the [[Force|forces]] acting on it can be described with them. Their mathematical representation depends on the [[Coordinate system|coordinate system]] used. The [[Dot product|dot product]] quantifies the angle between two vectors, and vectors are orthogonal when it is zero.

[[Clade]] of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] with two seed leaves (cotyledons) on germination. The name combines Greek *eu* ("true") with dicotyledon, and reflects that the group contains most plants considered dicots. Current names were introduced in 1991 by botanists James A. Doyle and Carol L. Hotton. Eudicots form one of the two largest clades of angiosperms, with over 70% of angiosperm species, and monocots are the other. Their pollen typically has three colpi, or grooves, which distinguish them from other seed plants. Familiar eudicots include the sunflower ([[Helianthus]]), dandelion ([[Taraxacum]]), [[Apple|apple]] and [[Maple|maple]], and most leafy, mid-latitude trees. Magnolias belong to the [[Magnoliids|magnoliids]] instead.

French Romantic painter and lithographer. Regarded as leader of the French Romantic school, and a friend and spiritual heir to Théodore Géricault, he was inspired by [[Peter Paul Rubens|Peter Paul Rubens]], Venetian painters and [[Lord Byron|Lord Byron]], favoring color and movement over clarity of outline. His expressive brushwork and study of the optical effects of color profoundly shaped the [[Impressionism|Impressionists]]. Dramatic works include *The Barque of Dante* (1822), *Massacre at Chios* (1824) and *Liberty Leading the People* (1830), which symbolizes the [[July Revolution]]. He painted murals for government commissions, including in the Palais Bourbon, and as a lithographer he illustrated works by [[William Shakespeare]], Walter Scott and [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]].

[[Novel]] in verse by [[Alexander Pushkin|Alexander Pushkin]], published serially from 1825 to 1832. Almost all of its 389 fourteen-line stanzas (5,446 lines) use iambic tetrameter in the so-called Onegin stanza, also called the Pushkin sonnet. Its title character, a bored St. Petersburg dandy who inherits an estate, has served as a model for Russian literary heroes known as superfluous men. He rejects Tatyana Larina's love letter, and after he flirts with Olga, Lensky's fiancée, at a ball, Lensky challenges him and Onegin kills him in a [[Duel|duel]]. Years later, he pursues the now-married Tatyana, who rejects him. The narrator's digressions on society, literature and dueling give the work its encyclopedic breadth.

Largely discredited set of beliefs and practices that aim to improve the genetic quality of a human population. Historically, eugenicists sought to alter the frequency of human traits by inhibiting the fertility of those deemed inferior, often through [[Sterilization (medicine)|forced sterilization]], or by promoting that of those deemed superior. [[Francis Galton]] coined the term in 1883, before [[Genetics]] was proposed as a discipline in 1906. A popular movement emerged in the United Kingdom in the late 19th century, but by the mid 20th century the term was closely associated with scientific racism and authoritarian coercion. Modern liberal eugenics rejects coercion in favor of individual parental choice.
